chapter: Leaving New York, jazz styles and religion
title: The New York stamp and Russell Smith's wife
summary: Many players flocked to New York for prestige, but Smith found no work there; Russell Smith saw his wife three days a year.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Why do you suppose, then, that these examples, in front of everybody (not just you; they were there for all to see)...
Why was it so many people, so many people from the colored race, wanted to be musicians? There were hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of them.
Yeah. The man at the union told me that there was 50 or 60 of them a week, coming in there from all parts of the world.
Why did they all want to do it?

Well, they come there because they're gettin' a stamp on themselves. Yeah, if they get the stamp on them, maybe that would make them...maybe they'd (?) everything and they'd have to bring(?) the dates out there, and they might get a break with some of those big agents to put some money behind them, so they might go on the road with a big band or something or another. All the nice bands. You can count 'em on one hand that were lucky enough where somebody, some big rich man put some money behind them, like John Hammond put some money behind Basie.

And the organ player, Ed Bachelor(?) in Kansas City, put the money behind McShann. But he didn't stay with it. He didn't care no more. He just kept it right there in Kansas City. That's why he didn't do too good.
Are you suggesting that in order to become established, a musician had to go to New York?
You couldn't do no good if you didn't go to New York.

Well, that's what they all figured. All the musicians figured that, that they couldn't do anything... You had to go to New York. You didn't stay. You got to go up there to the Apple and get that stamp on you, then you come out and then you have some prestige. Yeah, you've been to New York! I didn't let that bother me, heh-heh. Because I went on up there, however, and I'd seen what it was all about and everything, and I just seen that it wasn't nothin' but just a lay-down place. Just go there and you stayed. There wasn't no work there. You had to go out and make them circuits and tour around and be gone for two-three months, and when that's over with, you come back, sit down until they build up something else, and it's liable to be a half-year before they build up something else, and there you are. There was a trumpet player with Fletcher Henderson named Russell Smith.

That's right. Joe Smith's brother. And he rode with me. He was traveling with ...(?)... (?)..., and I stayed in (?) for about a month, and then I had to come back west. But he rode with me in my car. I was the only one that had a car. All the rest of the boys were in the bus. And he lived up on Sugar Hill, and he said he'd only seen his wife three days out of the year. Only with her three days out of the year. See, I didn't want that. I had my wife with me, riding with me. See, I wasn't going to go for that. I just wasn't used to that life, the way them people lived up there in Harlem in New York anyhow. I didn't like that.
